deep.reconstruction:
Notation. Euler writes ∫(1/z^m)(1/y^n) for Σ_{z≥1} z^{-m} Σ_{y≤z} y^{-n}. This is a non-strict ('star') double zeta value: ζ*(m,n) = ζ(m,n) + ζ(m+n), where ζ(m,n) = Σ_{z>y≥1} z^{-m} y^{-n}. He writes ∫1/z^k for ζ(k). The problem is to sum all series of a given weight w = m+n (Euler's 'ordo' w−1) in terms of ordinary zeta values.

Weight 9 (ordo octauus).
- First method (stuffle/reflection): ζ*(m,n) + ζ*(n,m) = ζ(m)ζ(n) + ζ(9) for m = 1..4. The m = 1 case is formal, since ζ(1) and ζ*(1,8) diverge.
- Second method. First result: ζ*(8,1) = 5ζ(9) − ζ(2)ζ(7) − ζ(3)ζ(6) − ζ(4)ζ(5). In strict form this is Euler's classical ζ(8,1) = 4ζ(9) − ½Σ_{k=1}^{6} ζ(k+1)ζ(8−k).
- Second method, two further linear relations (shuffle-type in effect):
  - 2ζ*(5,4) + 5ζ*(6,3) + 5ζ*(7,2) = 10ζ(3)ζ(6)
  - ζ*(6,3) + 3ζ*(7,2) = 6ζ(4)ζ(5) + 6ζ(3)ζ(6) − 10ζ(9)
- Counting: 8 series (m = 1..8, the m = 1 one only formally) against 7 equations. Euler concludes that one further independent evaluation, besides ζ*(8,1), would determine all of them.

Weight 10 (ordo nonus), first method only.
- ζ*(m,10−m) + ζ*(10−m,m) = ζ(m)ζ(10−m) + ζ(10) for m = 1..4.
- The symmetric case: ζ*(5,5) = ½ζ(5)² + ½ζ(10).
- The second-method results follow on the next page.
errors: No mathematical errors found. I checked numerically: ζ*(6,3) + 3ζ*(7,2) ≈ 4.05109, matching the right side ≈ 4.05109. Likewise 2ζ*(5,4) + 5ζ*(6,3) + 5ζ*(7,2) ≈ 12.22904 = 10ζ(3)ζ(6). The ζ*(8,1) formula agrees with Euler's known ζ(m,1) theorem.

The first equation in each order, ∫(1/z)(1/y^8) + ..., contains the divergent quantities ζ(1) and ζ*(1,8). It is purely formal, so the count '8 series vs 7 equations' really amounts to '7 convergent series vs 6 genuine relations'.

Euler's remark that one determination is still lacking is mathematically incomplete for odd weight 9. Every weight-9 double zeta value is in fact a polynomial in single zeta values; the missing relation follows from the full double-shuffle relations. This is a limitation of his method, not an error. For even weight 10 the gap is genuine, since ζ(7,3) is not reducible.

ideas.what: Reflection/stuffle formula ζ*(m,n) + ζ*(n,m) = ζ(m)ζ(n) + ζ(m+n)
ideas.modern_name: Stuffle (harmonic product) relation for double zeta values
ideas.where_published: E477, Novi Comm. Petrop. 20 (1776), §§ on 'methodus prima'

ideas.modern_name: Euler's formula for ζ(m,1) / linear Euler sums Σ H_n/n^m
ideas.where_published: E477; also E72-related work and the Goldbach correspondence

ideas.what: Additional linear relations among weight-9 double zetas from the 'second method'
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler; systematized by Borwein–Borwein–Girgensohn 1995 and Ihara–Kaneko–Zagier 2006

ideas.what: Counting argument: one missing relation per order
ideas.modern_name: Dimension of the space of double zeta values of weight w modulo products
ideas.usually_credited_to: Gangl–Kaneko–Zagier 2006 (connection to period polynomials / cusp forms)

missed.claim: Euler's 'one determination missing' is uniform across orders, but its status differs by parity. For odd weight 9 the missing relation exists, since all such values reduce to zeta products (Euler–Nielsen–Borwein et al.). For even weight ≥ 8 it is a genuine irreducible. Euler's counting is an early heuristic toward the dimension of the double zeta space. This is already discussed in modern commentaries on E477, so it is not new.
missed.quote: hae septem aequationes omnibus definiendis non sufficiunt; sin autem aliunde praeter seriem ∫1/z^8(1/y) vnica reliquarum summari posset, omnium plane summae hinc innotescerent
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical interest only. It shows Euler's methods did not by themselves prove the odd-weight reduction often attributed to him.

deep.surprise_reason: The formulas are correct and belong to Euler's well-studied double zeta work in E477, which is heavily cited in the MZV literature. Nothing here appears absent from the record.
transcription_corrections: Ordo nonus, fourth equation: the first term should be ∫1/z^4(1/y^6) (weight 10). The [?] can be resolved to z^4, although the print is blurred.
Ordo octauus, last line of first method: the stray mark before ∫1/z^9 is a plus sign: '+∫1/z^9'.
